notes:
AP Physics 1 - Ethan's notes

TOPIC 1: Newton's 2nd law + FBDs
- Fnet = ma, fnet is the VECTOR sum of all forces (not just one!!)
- always draw FBD 1st: Fg (mg, down), FN (perp to surface), Ft (tension), Ff (friction, opposes motion/ attempted motion), Fapp
- pick axes. on incline tilt axes so x is // to the ramp, y perp
- incline: Fg|| = mg sinθ, Fg⊥ = mg cosθ (sin goes w/ parallel, remember "slide = sin")
- FN = mg cosθ on incline (NOT always mg!!) Mrs O said this is a classic trap
- Friction: Ff ≤ μs FN (static), Ff = μk FN (kinetic)
- Ex: 5 kg box, 20 N push right, μk = 0.2 -> Ff = 0.2(5)(10) = 10 N -> Fnet = 10 N -> a = 2 m/s²
- Atwood: a = (m2 - m1)g/(m1 + m2), same a magnitude for both, tension same on both sides if pulley massless
- Newton's 3rd: forces on DIFFERENT objects, equal & opp, same type. so FN and Fg are NOT a 3rd law pair (common mistake)
- Apparent weight in elevator: accel up -> FN > mg, feel heavier

TOPIC 2: Work & energy
- W = F d cosθ (only the component // to displacement), units J = N·m
- W is + if force has component in direction of motion, - if opposite, 0 if perp (so FN and centripetal force do 0 work)
- KE = ½mv²
- Work-energy thm: Wnet = ΔKE
- Ex: 2 kg, v from 3 to 5 m/s -> ΔKE = ½(2)(25-9) = 16 J = Wnet
- Ug = mgh (h from chosen reference, only Δh matters)
- Us = ½kx² for spring, F = kx (Hooke's)
- Cons. of energy: Ki + Ui + Wext = Kf + Uf  (Wext includes friction as - work, becomes thermal)
- Power: P = W/t = Fv. unit W (watt). 1 hp ≈ 746 W
- speed at bottom of frictionless ramp = sqrt(2gh), mass doesnt matter!

TO STUDY b4 quiz 3: do packet #9 #4-12, redo roller coaster FRQ, memorize which forces do work on a pendulum (tension = 0 work, gravity does)
?? ask why Ff does neg work but still static friction can do + work (car accelerating)
photoText:
Work-Energy Theorem (textbook p. 214, photo taken at an angle)

The work done by the net force on an object equals the change in its kinetic energy:
Wnet = AKE = ½mvf² - ½mvi²

When a spring is compressed or stretched a distance x from its equiiibrium position, the spring force is F = -kx, where k is the spring constant in N/m. The elastic potential energy stored is Us = ½kx2 .

Example 6.4: A 0.50 kg block slides on a frictionless surface at 4.0 m/s and strikes a spring with k = 200 N/rn. How far is the spring compressed?
Solution: ½mv² = ½kx²
½(0.50)(4.0)² = ½(200)x²
4.0 J = 100 x²  ->  x = 0.20 rn

Note: Only conservative forces such as gravity and the spring force can be assigned a potential energy. [unreadable] is not conservative because the work depends on the path taken. Check units: N/m · m² = J.
transcript:
Okay, so, um, let's get settled, everybody. Phones away, please. Alright. So today we're talking about conservation of energy, and, uh, I want to really connect this back to what we did with the work-energy theorem last week.

So, the big idea. Energy isn't created or destroyed, right? It just moves around or changes form. So when we have a system, um, and nothing external is doing work on it, the total mechanical energy, that's kinetic plus potential, stays the same. So K initial plus U initial equals K final plus U final. Got it? And this will be on the exam, so write that down and put a box around it.

Now, let's do a, uh, a classic example. Picture a roller coaster car at the top of a hill. It's, um, let's say twenty meters up, and it starts basically from rest. So all of its energy at the top is, so, gravitational potential energy, m g h. Then it rolls down to the bottom, where h is zero. So now all of that potential energy has become kinetic energy, one half m v squared. Set them equal, and the mass cancels. You get v equals the square root of two g h. Plug in twenty meters, g about ten, and you get, um, the square root of four hundred, which is twenty meters per second. Does the mass matter? No. A heavy car and a light car, same speed at the bottom if there's no friction.

Oh, and sorry, completely random, but did anybody see the game on Friday night? I heard the band did a halftime show with, like, a whole drum line on the track. I wasn't there, my neighbor told me about it. Anyway. Back to physics.

So, what happens when there IS friction? Good question. Then mechanical energy is not conserved, so, um, we add a term. K initial plus U initial plus the work done by non-conservative forces equals K final plus U final. And the work done by friction is negative, because friction takes energy out and turns it into thermal energy, heat. The energy's not gone, it's just not mechanical anymore. So, so, if the car loses, say, a thousand joules to friction, the final kinetic energy is a thousand joules less than you'd get otherwise.

Let me do one with a spring now. A block, um, two kilograms, is pushed into a spring with k equal to five hundred newtons per meter, compressed point one meter. When released, how fast is the block moving as it leaves the spring on a frictionless table? Elastic potential energy is one half k x squared, so one half times five hundred times point oh one. That's two and a half joules. All that becomes kinetic. One half times two times v squared equals two point five. So v squared is two point five, v is about one point six meters per second. See how that works? Same strategy every time: pick your initial point, pick your final point, list the energies at each.

A common mistake, and I see this every year, is people forget to define where h equals zero. You can pick anywhere you want, it's your choice, but you have to stay consistent. Only changes in height matter.

Alright, announcements, before I forget. Quiz 3 is this coming Friday, October twenty-third, and it covers work, energy, and power. Also, your problem packet number nine is due Wednesday, so don't leave it for Tuesday night. I will be here for office hours Tuesday morning if you're stuck.

For the last few minutes, work with the person next to you on the pendulum problem on the board. Which forces do work? Tension or gravity? Talk it out, and I'll come around.
